title: Seoul Needs a Playbook for Hormuz, Ukraine, and What Comes Next
gist: South Korean lawmaker Jun-seok Lee and adviser Donghyeon Kim argue that simultaneous Trump administration pressure to send troops to the Strait of Hormuz and Cheongung-II air defense to Ukraine exposes Seoul's lack of principles; they propose a multilateral-legitimacy standard for deployments and a Lend-Lease-style statute with National Assembly notification for arms exports, citing polls showing public opposition to a Hormuz deployment.

insights.claim: The Trump administration is simultaneously pressuring South Korea to send troops to the Strait of Hormuz for the US-Iranian conflict and, via Trump sharing a Washington Post op-ed, to send its Cheongung-II air-defense system to Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Allied burden-sharing demands may redirect Korean defense output and naval assets.
insights.locator: Earlier this month, President Donald Trump

insights.claim: Seoul's Defense Ministry confirmed it sent a survey team to the Strait of Hormuz, with reported but unconfirmed assets including P-8A Poseidon aircraft, a naval EOD team and a logistics ship for surveillance to mine clearing.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Signals possible Korean participation in Hormuz mine-clearing operations.

insights.claim: The annual US-South Korea joint military exercise was abruptly canceled and downsized just weeks before the Hormuz deployment debate.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Suggests reduced alliance readiness on the peninsula.

insights.claim: Bilateral relations are further strained by a trade and tariff deal many South Koreans consider inherently unfair, and the salience of tariffs shows foreign policy is no longer insulated from domestic politics.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Tariff grievances constrain Seoul's willingness to support US asks.
insights.locator: From Ad Hoc Decisions to Strategy

insights.claim: South Korea receives nearly two-thirds of its oil and one-fifth of its LNG imports through the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Korea's energy security is directly exposed to the US-Iran conflict.
insights.quote: receives nearly two-thirds of its oil and one-fifth of its liquefied natural gas imports through it
insights.locator: When Should South Korea Send Troops?

insights.claim: Iran supplied 13.2 percent of South Korea's oil imports as recently as 2017, and South Korea held roughly $6 billion in frozen Iranian oil revenue from 2018 to 2023.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Seoul retains independent economic equities with Tehran that complicate alignment.
insights.quote: As recently as 2017, Iran supplied 13.2 percent of South Korea’s oil imports

insights.claim: China buys as much as 90 percent of Iran's oil exports, making it far more exposed to Hormuz disruption than South Korea, and has used economic retaliation against Seoul over THAAD before.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Chinese retaliation risk is a factor for Korean firms if Seoul aligns with US operations.
insights.quote: China buys as much as 90 percent of Iran’s oil exports

insights.claim: Russia's foreign ministry threatened 'asymmetric' retaliatory measures when Seoul considered joining a NATO-led initiative to buy US weapons for Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Russian retaliation risk constrains Korean arms support to Ukraine.

insights.claim: A Sept. 7 Reform Institute poll found 62.4 percent of South Koreans called the US Hormuz request unjustified, while an independent four-firm survey found 45 percent opposed versus 36 percent in favor.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Domestic opposition makes a Korean Hormuz deployment uncertain.

insights.claim: When forced to prioritize, 41.4 percent wanted neither a Hormuz deployment nor Ukraine arms support, while coalition-only participation was the preferred form of any involvement and 84 percent wanted prior National Assembly deliberation.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Coalition framing is the politically viable path for any Korean contribution.
insights.locator: The Reform Institute poll also found

insights.claim: The ruling party is ambivalent about the mission's clarity and necessity, making it uncertain whether the government can secure National Assembly consent.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: A deployment vote could fail or be delayed.

insights.claim: South Korea should deploy troops abroad only with multilateral legitimacy, either a recognized coalition or a basis in international law such as a UN resolution, peacekeeping mandate or freedom-of-navigation right.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Would make Korean alliance contributions more predictable but conditional.

insights.claim: With North Korea gaining missile and reconnaissance technology from Russia and Korean exercises scaled back, Seoul has good reason to keep military capacity concentrated on the peninsula rather than in the Persian Gulf.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Peninsula threat environment limits Korea's out-of-area contributions.

insights.claim: The Cheonghae destroyer is configured for anti-piracy rather than drone and mine threats, and transit from Korea takes about a month, undermining logistical feasibility of a Hormuz deployment.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Korea's practical naval contribution would be limited.

insights.claim: In 2020 Seoul expanded its Cheonghae unit's area of operation into the Gulf to help the US without joining the IMSC, bypassing National Assembly consent, a move the authors say cannot be repeated during a hot war.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: The ambiguity hedge is no longer available to Seoul.

insights.claim: Immediate Cheongung-II export to Ukraine is limited by Seoul's policy against arming parties in active conflict and by supply shortages tied to existing contracts.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Korean air-defense order backlogs are already tight.
insights.locator: A Framework for Arming Partners at War

insights.claim: South Korea's restrictions on arms exports to warring parties sit at the enforcement decree or ministerial level, so the government can loosen them by cabinet decision without a National Assembly vote.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Policy on Korean arms exports to Ukraine could change quickly, a swing factor for Korean defense exporters.
insights.quote: the government can tighten or loosen them by cabinet or ministerial decision alone, without a National Assembly vote
insights.locator: A Framework for Arming Partners at War

insights.claim: Unlike US Foreign Military Sales under congressional notification, Korean arms exports are authorized administratively by DAPA with no National Assembly role; the authors propose a statutory notification-and-objection window.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Added legislative oversight could slow or politicize Korean defense export deals.

insights.claim: The authors propose a Lend-Lease-style statute tying aid to a partner's centrality to the rules-based order or Korea's supply-chain stability, giving predictability while avoiding co-belligerency.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: A statutory framework could unlock larger, steadier Korean defense exports.

insights.claim: South Korea's defense industry has grown significantly over the past decade and is projected to keep growing, but its exports are inherently entangled with foreign policy.
insights.speaker: Jun-seok Lee and Donghyeon Kim
insights.so_what: Korean defense exporters face policy risk alongside structural growth.
